claims.text: The as-cast eutectic AlCoCrFeNi alloy has a dual-phase microstructure consisting of ductile FCC and brittle B2 phases.
Adding approximately 1–2 at.% Nb during melting, followed by homogenization and controlled cooling, will produce fine, uniformly distributed Nb-rich secondary particles.
The Nb-rich secondary particles will preferentially occur along eutectic phase boundaries.
A short homogenization treatment at 1100°C will help prevent coarsening of the Nb-rich particles.
Nb-rich particles will pin or impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion will increase yield strength.
Nb-rich particles at phase boundaries will reinforce interphase cohesion.
Reinforced interphase cohesion will improve load transfer between phases.
Reinforced interphase cohesion will delay localized failure.
The Nb-containing microstructure will produce a more uniform strain distribution.
The Nb-added alloy will have higher yield strength than the alloy without Nb.
The Nb-added alloy will have greater ductility than the alloy without Nb.
Nb contents significantly above 2 at.% may cause Nb-rich particle coarsening.
Major deviations from the proposed heat-treatment protocol may cause Nb-rich particle coarsening.
Coarsening or uneven distribution of Nb-rich particles may cause embrittlement.

contradictions.description: The baseline is described as using conventional heat-treatment methods, whereas the falsification experiment subjects both the Nb-added and baseline samples to the same optimized short homogenization treatment. These define different baseline processing histories.

The hypothesis presents Nb addition together with optimized homogenization and controlled cooling as a combined intervention, but the experiment holds the optimized heat treatment constant and isolates only Nb addition. Thus, the proposed intervention and the intervention actually tested are not defined consistently.
